course.title: AP World History: Modern
course.description: Understand the people, ideas, and connections that shaped the world from c. 1200 to the present.
course.previewDescription: Explore how states rose, belief systems spread, trade networks connected regions, and revolutions reshaped societies from c. 1200 to the present.

unit.title: The Global Tapestry
unit.description: Explore how societies organized power, shared beliefs, and built their economies across the world.

framework.name: InSPECT
framework.title: Use InSPECT to choose your evidence
framework.intro: A fact can connect to more than one lens. Choose the lens that helps answer the prompt.
framework.sourceNote: Based on the class Early Religions + InSPECT slides, pages 5-17.

themes.title: Interactions of humans with the environment
themes.question: How did geography, crops, resources, or disease shape choices?
themes.example: Andean terraces made steep slopes more usable for farming.

themes.title: Social interactions and organization
themes.question: Who had status, opportunities, or obligations?
themes.example: Examination preparation favored families that could afford education.

themes.title: Political systems and governance
themes.question: How did rulers gain authority and administer territory?
themes.example: Song officials carried imperial decisions into local government.

themes.title: Economic systems
themes.question: How were goods produced, exchanged, taxed, or distributed?
themes.example: Mali drew revenue from commerce through its territory.

themes.title: Cultural developments and interactions
themes.question: How did beliefs, learning, and artistic practices influence society?
themes.example: Buddhist monasteries connected religious practice with education.

themes.title: Technology and innovation
themes.question: What techniques or tools changed what people could do?
themes.example: Inca roads and knotted records helped officials coordinate resources.

questions.prompt: Why did conversion to Islam not necessarily remove a person’s low social status in South Asia?
choices: Islamic law in South Asia formally assigned converts to the caste of their ancestors
Muslim rulers required converts to pay higher taxes than other subjects
Local hierarchies also rested on occupation, wealth, and inherited community ties
Converts were barred from mosques until their families had been Muslim for generations
questions.explanation: Status depended on more than religion. Occupation, wealth, and jati ties persisted after conversion.

sourceLocators.locator: Topic 1.3 learning objectives and historical developments

choiceExplanations: Islam did not formally assign caste, but social practice often carried earlier hierarchies forward; that persistence is the point.
The jizya fell on non-Muslims, not converts, so taxation does not explain lasting low status.
Status depended on more than religion. Occupation, wealth, and jati ties persisted after conversion.
No such general rule existed; converts joined Muslim worship.
questions.distinguisher: Ask what else, besides religion, determined status.

questions.prompt: What best explains the coexistence of the Delhi Sultanate, Rajput kingdoms, and Vijayanagara?
choices: Regional rulers kept separate power bases, and no one state could control the subcontinent
The Delhi Sultanate appointed Rajput and Vijayanagara rulers as its provincial governors
Religious law forbade Hindu and Muslim rulers from fighting one another
Regional rulers kept separate power bases because Mongol rule had divided India into khanates
questions.explanation: Each relied on its own armies, revenue, and alliances, and none could absorb the others.

sourceLocators.locator: Topic 1.3 learning objectives and historical developments

choiceExplanations: Each relied on its own armies, revenue, and alliances, and none could absorb the others.
Rajput kingdoms and Vijayanagara were independent rivals, not sultanate provinces.
These states did fight, and alliances crossed religious lines when politics required.
Separate power bases are right, but the Mongols never conquered India; the sultanate repelled their invasions.
questions.distinguisher: Fragmentation came from regional strength, not from an outside conqueror.

questions.prompt: Which comparison of Bhakti and Sufi traditions is most defensible?
choices: Both spread mainly through the conquests of the Delhi Sultanate's armies
Both emphasized personal devotion and abolished caste among their followers
Both rejected the larger religions they grew from and formed new faiths
Both emphasized personal devotion and often taught in local languages
questions.explanation: Each stressed a direct, devotional relationship with the divine and reached people beyond religious specialists.

sourceLocators.locator: Topic 1.3 learning objectives and historical developments

choiceExplanations: Sufis traveled with or after armies at times, but both spread mainly through teachers and communities.
Some Bhakti teachers criticized caste, but neither movement abolished hierarchy.
Bhakti stayed within Hindu traditions and Sufism within Islam.
Each stressed a direct, devotional relationship with the divine and reached people beyond religious specialists.
questions.distinguisher: A shared emphasis does not mean a shared result such as ending caste.

questions.prompt: How could a ruler of a Southeast Asian port convert location into political power?
choices: By attracting ships and forcing every merchant to adopt the ruler's religion
By attracting ships, collecting port revenue, and protecting merchants
By closing the port to foreigners so local farmers controlled all trade
By building a road network that replaced sea travel across the region
questions.explanation: Revenue and good relations with traders turned a strategic harbor into wealth and influence.

sourceLocators.locator: Topic 1.3 learning objectives and historical developments

choiceExplanations: Attracting ships is right, but forced conversion would drive merchants to rival ports.
Revenue and good relations with traders turned a strategic harbor into wealth and influence.
Closing the port would remove the revenue that made location valuable.
Maritime Southeast Asia depended on sea routes; roads could not replace them.
questions.distinguisher: Location becomes power only when rulers organize revenue and keep merchants coming.

questions.prompt: What do Khmer reservoirs and canals most directly help explain?
choices: The defensive moats that protected Angkor from all foreign invasions
The farm surplus that supported Angkor's population and building projects
The navigation routes that linked Angkor directly to Chinese ports
The trade surplus that Angkor earned by exporting water to its neighbors
questions.explanation: Water management helped grow rice for a large population and freed labor for temples and the state.

sourceLocators.locator: Topic 1.3 learning objectives and historical developments

choiceExplanations: Some waterworks had defensive uses, but Angkor was attacked and later abandoned as a capital.
Water management helped grow rice for a large population and freed labor for temples and the state.
The waterworks served agriculture, not direct sea access to China.
Water supported farming at Angkor; it was not an export.
questions.distinguisher: Follow water to rice, and rice to people and power.

questions.prompt: A temple built for Vishnu later becomes a Buddhist place of worship. What does this change best illustrate?
choices: Buddhism and Hinduism were the same religion under different names
Religious practice changed because Khmer rulers banned Hinduism by law
Most residents of the region migrated away and were replaced by newcomers
Religious practice could change while an important site kept its significance
questions.explanation: Angkor Wat's use changed, but it remained a major sacred and political site.

sourceLocators.locator: Topic 1.3 learning objectives and historical developments

choiceExplanations: They share some ideas but are distinct traditions.
Royal patronage shifted toward Buddhism, but the change was gradual, not a legal ban.
A change of worship does not show population replacement.
Angkor Wat's use changed, but it remained a major sacred and political site.
questions.distinguisher: Continuity of place, change of practice.

questions.prompt: Why could temple patronage help Vijayanagara rulers maintain authority?
choices: It linked rulers to sacred tradition and to temples that controlled land and wealth
It linked rulers to sacred tradition, which ended the need for armies or taxes
It required all subjects to join a single temple and worship one deity
It persuaded the Delhi Sultanate to recognize Vijayanagara's independence
questions.explanation: Temples were religious centers and major landholders, so patronage brought legitimacy and resources.

sourceLocators.locator: Topic 1.3 learning objectives and historical developments

choiceExplanations: Temples were religious centers and major landholders, so patronage brought legitimacy and resources.
Legitimacy mattered, but Vijayanagara also relied on armies and land revenue.
Hindu practice was diverse; patronage did not impose a single cult.
Vijayanagara's independence rested on military power, not sultanate recognition.
questions.distinguisher: Patronage supported authority alongside, not instead of, force and revenue.

questions.prompt: Which evidence would best support a claim that Buddhism connected politically separate societies?
choices: A single Buddhist king ruling over both Sri Lanka and mainland Southeast Asia at once
Hindu temples built at Angkor in honor of Vishnu in the 1100s
Monks traveling between Sri Lanka and mainland Southeast Asia for ordination
Monks living in one Sukhothai monastery and teaching only local students
questions.explanation: Travel for study and ordination shows religious ties crossing political borders.

sourceLocators.locator: Topic 1.3 learning objectives and historical developments

choiceExplanations: No single king ruled both, which is why the claim stresses separate societies.
Hindu temples do not provide evidence about Buddhist connections.
Travel for study and ordination shows religious ties crossing political borders.
Monastic life in one place shows local practice, not connections between societies.
questions.distinguisher: Evidence must show a connection across borders.

choices: Strict study of Sanskrit legal texts
Ritual led only by Brahmin priests
Withdrawal from society into monasteries
Personal devotion to a deity
questions.explanation: Bhakti centers on a loving, personal relationship with a chosen deity.

sourceLocators.locator: Topic 1.3 learning objectives and historical developments

choiceExplanations: Bhakti poets often wrote in local languages rather than Sanskrit.
Bhakti often bypassed priestly ritual, using local languages and song.
Monastic withdrawal is associated more with Buddhism.
Bhakti centers on a loving, personal relationship with a chosen deity.

questions.prompt: Which description of Majapahit is accurate?
choices: A Sumatran Buddhist maritime power with roots well before 1200
A Muslim sultanate that controlled the Strait of Malacca
A Javanese state with Hindu and Buddhist court traditions
A Khmer kingdom centered on the temples of Angkor
questions.explanation: Majapahit, founded on Java in 1293, blended Hindu and Buddhist traditions with maritime ties.

sourceLocators.locator: Topic 1.3 learning objectives and historical developments

choiceExplanations: That describes Srivijaya, an earlier Buddhist power based on Sumatra.
That describes Melaka in the 1400s.
Majapahit, founded on Java in 1293, blended Hindu and Buddhist traditions with maritime ties.
Angkor was the Khmer capital on the mainland, not on Java.
questions.distinguisher: Separate the Southeast Asian states by place and period.

questions.prompt: Which pair connects a place to a relevant institution?
choices: Vijayanagara and the Theravada monastic order
Sinhala kingdoms and Buddhist monastic patronage
Majapahit and the Delhi Sultanate's land revenue
Sukhothai and Hindu temple patronage to Vishnu
questions.explanation: Sinhala rulers in Sri Lanka supported Buddhist monasteries and irrigation.

sourceLocators.locator: Topic 1.3 learning objectives and historical developments

choiceExplanations: Vijayanagara patronized Hindu temples.
Sinhala rulers in Sri Lanka supported Buddhist monasteries and irrigation.
Majapahit was a Javanese state; the Delhi Sultanate ruled northern India.
Sukhothai rulers supported Theravada Buddhism, not mainly Vishnu temples.
questions.distinguisher: Match each state with its main religious institution.

questions.prompt: According to the passage, Islam spread in Ferlec mainly through
choices: contact with Muslim merchants in the hill country
the conquest of the kingdom by a Muslim army
contact with Muslim merchants in the towns
the orders of a ruler appointed by the Great Kaan
questions.explanation: Polo says Saracen merchants frequented Ferlec and converted the townspeople.
choiceExplanations: Polo specifies “the townspeople only,” excluding the hill people.
Polo names merchants, not an army, as the cause of conversion.
Polo says Saracen merchants frequented Ferlec and converted the townspeople.
The Great Kaan's men could not even reach these islands, according to the passage.
questions.distinguisher: Merchants are the right agents, but Polo limits conversion to townspeople, not the hill people.

stimulusBlocks.attribution: Marco Polo, Venetian merchant who traveled in Mongol-ruled Asia c. 1271–1295, account dictated to the writer Rustichello of Pisa, c. 1298, describing northern Sumatra, which he passed on his voyage home, c. 1292
stimulusBlocks.citation: The Book of Ser Marco Polo, trans. Henry Yule, rev. Henri Cordier, 3rd ed. (London: John Murray, 1903), vol. 2, Book III, ch. 9. Project Gutenberg eBook #12410.
stimulusBlocks.note: “Java the Less” is Sumatra. Ferlec is Perlak, on Sumatra's northern tip. Saracen means Muslim; “Idolaters” was the translator's term for followers of Buddhist and Hindu traditions. Bracketed words replace “This” at the start of a sentence about the next kingdom.
stimulusBlocks.text:
You see there are upon it eight kingdoms and eight crowned kings. The people are all Idolaters, and every kingdom has a language of its own. The Island hath great abundance of treasure, with costly spices, lign-aloes and spikenard and many others that never come into our parts. . . .

This kingdom, you must know, is so much frequented by the Saracen merchants that they have converted the natives to the Law of Mahommet--I mean the townspeople only . . . .

[Basma] also is an independent kingdom, and the people have a language of their own . . . . They call themselves subjects of the Great Kaan, but they pay him no tribute; indeed they are so far away that his men could not go thither. Still all these Islanders declare themselves to be his subjects, and sometimes they send him curiosities as presents.

questions.prompt: Which of the following best explains why the process described in the passage occurred in coastal towns first?
choices: Ports were visited regularly by merchants who belonged to Indian Ocean Muslim networks
Coastal rulers were forced to convert by the Delhi Sultanate's navy
Muslim scholars avoided inland areas because of strict local laws
Ports were visited regularly by merchants who were required by law to convert local rulers
questions.explanation: Regular trade brought Muslim merchants and teachers to ports, where conversion could also ease commercial ties.
choiceExplanations: Regular trade brought Muslim merchants and teachers to ports, where conversion could also ease commercial ties.
The Delhi Sultanate was a land-based state in northern India and did not conquer Sumatra.
The passage gives no evidence of such laws; access, not prohibition, explains the coastal pattern.
Merchants spread Islam through contact and community, not under any requirement to convert rulers.
questions.distinguisher: Merchant contact explains the pattern, but no rule required merchants to convert rulers; conversion was voluntary and gradual.

questions.prompt: Polo's description of Basma's relationship with the Great Kaan is best understood in the context of
choices: Chinese tribute relationships in which distant rulers paid heavy annual taxes
the spread of Christianity among Southeast Asian islanders
the Mongol conquest and direct rule of maritime Southeast Asia
Chinese tribute relationships in which distant rulers sent gifts as a sign of respect
questions.explanation: Rulers declared themselves subjects and sent presents, a symbolic relationship common in Chinese diplomacy.
choiceExplanations: The passage says Basma's people pay the Kaan no tribute.
The passage mentions Islam and local beliefs, not Christianity.
Polo says the Kaan's men could not reach Basma, so there was no direct rule.

questions.prompt: The passage provides evidence for which of the following?
choices: Buddhist and Muslim pilgrims agreed that the mountain held the Buddha's tomb
Buddhist and Muslim pilgrims both treated the same mountain as sacred
Muslim rulers had forced Buddhists in Sri Lanka to abandon pilgrimage
Christian missionaries had converted most of the people of Sri Lanka
questions.explanation: Polo says Idolaters (Buddhists) and Saracens (Muslims) both come on pilgrimage to the mountain.
choiceExplanations: Muslims identified the site as Adam's tomb, not the Buddha's.
Polo says Idolaters (Buddhists) and Saracens (Muslims) both come on pilgrimage to the mountain.
The passage shows both groups making pilgrimages, not one forcing the other out.
Polo compares the pilgrimage to a Christian shrine in Spain; he does not describe Christians in Sri Lanka.
questions.distinguisher: Both groups revered the site, but Polo says each identified it differently: the Buddha for one, Adam for the other.

stimulusBlocks.attribution: Marco Polo, Venetian merchant who traveled in Mongol-ruled Asia c. 1271–1295, account dictated to the writer Rustichello of Pisa, c. 1298, describing Adam's Peak in Sri Lanka
stimulusBlocks.citation: The Book of Ser Marco Polo, trans. Henry Yule, rev. Henri Cordier, 3rd ed. (London: John Murray, 1903), vol. 2, Book III, ch. 15. Project Gutenberg eBook #12410.
stimulusBlocks.note: Seilan is Sri Lanka. Sagamoni Borcan is Shakyamuni Buddha; “Idolaters” was the translator's term for Buddhists. Saracens means Muslims. Gallicia is Galicia, in Spain, where Christians visited the shrine of Saint James.
stimulusBlocks.text:
Furthermore you must know that in the Island of Seilan there is an exceeding high mountain . . . . And I tell you they say that on this mountain is the sepulchre of Adam our first parent; at least that is what the Saracens say. But the Idolaters say that it is the sepulchre of SAGAMONI BORCAN, before whose time there were no idols. They hold him to have been the best of men, a great saint in fact, according to their fashion, and the first in whose name idols were made. . . .

The Idolaters come thither on pilgrimage from very long distances and with great devotion, just as Christians go to the shrine of Messer Saint James in Gallicia. . . . But the Saracens also come thither on pilgrimage in great numbers, and they say that it is the sepulchre of Adam our first father, and that the teeth, and the hair, and the dish were those of Adam.

questions.prompt: Polo's comparison of the pilgrimage to the shrine of Saint James in Gallicia most likely reflects
choices: his belief that Buddhism and Christianity were the same religion
his effort to explain an unfamiliar practice to European readers
his effort to convince Buddhists to visit Christian shrines
his belief that pilgrimage was unknown in Europe
questions.explanation: Polo wrote for Europeans and used a familiar Christian pilgrimage to make the practice understandable.
choiceExplanations: Polo still calls the Buddhists Idolaters, so he clearly saw the religions as different.
Polo wrote for Europeans and used a familiar Christian pilgrimage to make the practice understandable.
Polo's audience was European, not Buddhist.
Polo's comparison only works because Europeans already knew pilgrimage well.
questions.distinguisher: The comparison is about the practice of pilgrimage. Polo still calls the Buddhists “Idolaters,” so he did not think the religions were the same.

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, which of the following was a similarity between the Delhi Sultanate and the Vijayanagara Empire?
choices: Both converted most of their subjects to the rulers' religion
Both were founded by Turkic and Afghan military elites
Both relied on trade revenue rather than agricultural taxes
Both relied on agricultural revenue to support their armies
questions.explanation: The Delhi sultans collected land revenue and Vijayanagara built power on agricultural revenue, each funding a large army.
choiceExplanations: The passage says most of the Sultanate's subjects did not convert.
Only the Delhi Sultanate was founded by Turkic and Afghan elites.
Both used land revenue; trade was an addition, not a replacement.
The Delhi sultans collected land revenue and Vijayanagara built power on agricultural revenue, each funding a large army.
questions.distinguisher: Vijayanagara did profit from trade, but the passage says both states depended on land or agricultural revenue.

stimulusBlocks.source: CED Topic 1.3, KC-3.2.I.B.i: new Hindu and Buddhist states emerged in South and Southeast Asia, alongside Muslim-ruled states
stimulusBlocks.attribution: Practice passage written for Page One, comparing states in South Asia, c. 1200–1450
stimulusBlocks.text:
The Delhi Sultanate, founded in 1206, was ruled by Turkic and Afghan Muslim elites who governed a mostly Hindu population. Sultans relied on cavalry armies and on land revenue collected through local intermediaries, and they faced constant pressure from regional rivals. Most of their subjects did not convert to Islam.

Farther south, the Vijayanagara Empire, founded in 1336, built its power on agricultural revenue, trade, and a large army. Its rulers presented themselves as protectors of Hindu tradition and gave rich gifts to temples, which in turn served as centers of worship, landholding, and local economic life.

questions.prompt: The passage best supports which of the following conclusions about South Asia in this period?
choices: Political power was divided among rival states with different religious traditions
The Delhi Sultanate unified the subcontinent under a single Muslim government
Hindu temples lost their economic role after the arrival of Muslim rulers
Political power was divided among states that all shared one religious tradition
questions.explanation: A Muslim-ruled sultanate in the north and a Hindu-patron empire in the south competed for power.
choiceExplanations: A Muslim-ruled sultanate in the north and a Hindu-patron empire in the south competed for power.
The passage stresses regional rivals and a separate southern empire, not unification.
Vijayanagara temples remained centers of landholding and economic life.
The two states had different ruling religions, so they did not share one tradition.
questions.distinguisher: Power was divided, but the passage contrasts a Muslim-ruled sultanate with a Hindu-patron empire.

questions.prompt: Which of the following best explains why Vijayanagara rulers gave rich gifts to temples?
choices: Temples were the only institutions that could train soldiers
Temple patronage strengthened rulers' claims to be descended from the Buddha himself
Temple patronage strengthened rulers' legitimacy and ties to local economic life
Temples were required by Delhi sultans to pay tribute on the rulers' behalf

Vijayanagara rulers claimed to protect Hindu tradition, not descent from the Buddha.
Supporting temples presented kings as protectors of Hindu tradition and linked them to centers of land and wealth.
